name: The Grid's New Landlords
overview_deck: Gas pipelines, midstream networks, and utility transmission operators are quietly becoming the indispensable infrastructure beneath the AI economy — collecting tolls on electrons and molecules that neither hyperscalers nor renewable developers can route around.

angles.title: The Reliability Gap That Handed Gas the Keys
angles.focus: For a decade, the energy-transition narrative assumed renewables plus storage would displace gas before AI demand landed. The 2025-2026 data-center buildout revealed the gap: intermittent generation cannot guarantee the continuous, firm megawatts hyperscalers require at scale, and the infrastructure that can — gas transmission, storage, and behind-the-meter generation — was already built, depreciated, and owned by a handful of corridor operators. This page traces how a power-reliability problem became an infrastructure-rent problem.
angles.key_question: Why did gas infrastructure emerge as the floor beneath the AI power buildout rather than being bypassed by renewables?

groups.group_title: Four Ways to Collect the Toll

angles.title: From Pipeline to Power Platform: The Gas-Transmission Play
angles.focus: Williams Companies is the clearest case of a gas-transmission operator deliberately morphing into a power-infrastructure platform. Its Transco interstate system already carried roughly one-third of U.S. natural gas; now the Blackstone power-innovation JV, Socrates, and Power Express projects add behind-the-meter generation and data-center power supply to the same footprint. The bet is that gas transmission plus on-site power capability creates a new toll layer that neither pure-pipeline nor pure-power competitors can replicate.
angles.key_question: How does a gas-pipeline operator convert existing corridor control into a power-delivery product for hyperscalers and industrial customers?

angles.title: The Molecule Machine: NGL, Fractionation, and Export Corridor Control
angles.focus: Energy Transfer and Enterprise Products Partners represent a different toll model: not power delivery but molecule logistics — controlling the chain from Permian basin gathering through fractionation at Mont Belvieu to NGL export docks at Nederland. Long-term agreements extending into the 2030s, record NGL volumes, and new fractionation capacity mean these operators collect margin at every link in a chain that neither upstream producers nor downstream buyers can bypass. The AI economy's indirect dependency runs through the petrochemical and industrial feedstock demand that competes for the same corridor capacity.
angles.key_question: How do integrated NGL and export-corridor operators capture structural rent across a chain of linked bottlenecks rather than a single tariff schedule?

angles.title: The Regional Utility as Data-Center Landlord
angles.focus: Alliant Energy's Iowa and Wisconsin footprint illustrates how regulated utilities with the right geographic proximity and regulatory flexibility are being transformed by data-center siting. With 3.4 GW of contracted large-load demand and a projected 60% peak-load increase by 2031, Alliant is building a $13.4B capital plan justified entirely by signed ESAs with QTS, Google, and Meta. The regulated compact converts hyperscaler growth into predictable rate-base returns — and shifts construction and financing risk to ratepayers.
angles.key_question: How does a mid-sized regulated utility convert proximity to AI campus corridors into a decade-long capital-compounding program?

angles.title: The Quiet Compounder: Gas Distribution as Rate-Base Machine
angles.focus: Atmos Energy and its peers represent the least visible toll-collector: local gas distribution and intrastate pipeline operators whose rate bases double through modernization spend alone, without needing a single hyperscaler contract. Atmos projects $26B of capex through FY2030 and rate-base growth from $21.4B to $42B on the back of safety and reliability upgrades — a compounding model that exists because regulators allow capital recovery on a system the AI economy cannot afford to let fail.
angles.key_question: How do gas-distribution utilities compound rate base and earnings without direct AI demand exposure, simply by being irreplaceable delivery infrastructure?

angles.title: Williams Companies: Portrait of a Toll Road Becoming a Power Utility
angles.focus: Williams is the single company that most clearly shows what happens when a gas-transmission operator decides to become an AI-economy power provider. This page dissects the full evolution: Transco's interstate dominance, the Gulf Coast and deepwater gathering expansion, the Haynesville positioning via Momentum Midstream, and the Blackstone JV that formalizes the behind-the-meter power strategy. The $8.4B 2026 EBITDA guidance raise — $200M attributable to power innovation — is the clearest financial proof that the toll-road is charging a new rate.
angles.key_question: What does it look like, in financial and operational detail, when a natural-gas pipeline company successfully pivots its identity toward AI-economy power infrastructure?

angles.title: Who Actually Pays for the AI Power Buildout
angles.focus: The capex that utilities and pipeline operators are deploying to serve data-center demand is not borne by hyperscalers alone. In regulated markets, construction costs flow into rate bases and are recovered through electricity and gas bills paid by households, small businesses, and industrial customers who receive no share of AI economic gains. Communities near new transmission routes and pipeline expansions absorb siting disruption, construction noise, and environmental risk without pricing power. This page maps the burden-transfer from the stated beneficiaries to the actual bill-payers.
angles.key_question: Which households and communities fund the infrastructure buildout for AI, and what mechanisms transfer the cost from hyperscalers to rate-payers?

angles.title: The Stranded Asset Trap: What Breaks If AI Demand Disappoints
angles.focus: Every $13B capital plan and every raised EBITDA guidance is premised on contracted AI demand materializing and persisting for decades. If hyperscaler buildout slows, model efficiency reduces power intensity, or the regulatory compact shifts, the capex already committed becomes stranded — absorbed by equity holders and ratepayers rather than the customers who signed the agreements. Energy Transfer's decision to suspend Lake Charles LNG in favor of natural-gas infrastructure offers a case study in what capital-allocation regret looks like when a demand thesis stalls; this page applies the same skeptic's lens to the AI-power buildout.
angles.key_question: What is the mechanism by which optimistic AI-demand assumptions translate into stranded assets, and who absorbs the loss when contracted load fails to materialize?
